sections.description: This section introduces the patient's background, preoperative course, cardiac surgery, and the development of postoperative thrombocytopenia with neurological complications. It sets the clinical stage by explaining how preoperative heparin exposure during heart catheterization set the temporal framework for an unusually early onset of HIT, and how the postoperative platelet count decline and stroke prompted further investigation.
subtopics: Patient demographics, comorbidities (atrial fibrillation on apixaban, exertional dyspnea, aortic stenosis)
Preoperative heart catheterization with low-dose UFH (2000 U) via transradial approach
Cardiac surgery details: aortic valve replacement, ascending aorta replacement, CABG, left atrial appendage excision with intraoperative UFH (45,000 U)
Postoperative platelet count trajectory: baseline 210×10⁹/L → POD1 155×10⁹/L → progressive decline to 50×10⁹/L on POD5
Postoperative thromboprophylaxis with LMWH (dalteparin) from POD1 to POD4
Worsening postoperative delirium and discovery of acute left parietal lobe cerebral infarct on CT imaging on POD6
Concept of early-onset HIT (before POD5) and its association with recent preoperative heparin exposure
Clinical significance of thrombosis (stroke) accompanying thrombocytopenia as a hallmark of HIT

sections.section_title: Differential Diagnosis and Initial Laboratory Evaluation
sections.description: This section covers the systematic approach to diagnosing the cause of severe post-cardiac surgery thrombocytopenia. It explains how clinicians evaluated and ruled out common and rare causes of thrombocytopenia in this context, and how the combination of clinical features, routine laboratory results, and identification of preoperative heparin exposure pointed toward HIT as the most probable diagnosis.
subtopics: Common causes of post-cardiac surgery thrombocytopenia: cardiogenic shock/critical illness, infection
Rare causes of post-cardiac surgery thrombocytopenia: post-transfusion purpura, post-surgical TTP, drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia
Initial laboratory workup: complete blood count, hemoglobin stability, normal white blood cell count and differential
Coagulation studies: normal PT/INR, normal PTT, elevated fibrinogen as acute phase reactant
Markers ruling out hemolysis: normal haptoglobin, normal reticulocyte count, initial absence of schistocytes
Blood and urine cultures to exclude infection, chest X-ray findings
Peripheral blood film review confirming true thrombocytopenia without platelet clumps
Temporal reasoning: ruling out drug-induced thrombocytopenia based on onset timing relative to newly administered drugs
Recognition that preoperative UFH at heart catheterization provided the necessary antecedent exposure for early-onset HIT
Decision to send HIT antibody testing to reference laboratory

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology and Laboratory Diagnosis of Classic HIT vs. Autoimmune HIT
sections.description: This section explains the immunopathophysiology of classic HIT and how autoimmune HIT (aHIT) differs, then details the laboratory tests used to diagnose HIT, with emphasis on interpreting the atypical serotonin-release assay (SRA) results that were critical to identifying this case as aHIT. It covers the PF4/polyanion ELISA, the SRA, the role of Fc receptor blockade with monoclonal antibody IV.3, and the novel serological phenotype of partial Fc receptor blockade resistance.
subtopics: Pathophysiology of classic HIT: PF4-heparin immune complexes, IgG antibodies, platelet Fc receptor (FcγRIIa) clustering and activation
Concept of autoimmune HIT (aHIT): heparin-independent platelet activation by HIT antibodies
Clinical features distinguishing aHIT from classic HIT: severe thrombocytopenia, delayed platelet recovery, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)-like features
PF4/polyanion ELISA: principle, interpretation, and the strongly positive result (2.2 OD units) in this case
Serotonin-release assay (SRA): principle, diagnostic criteria, and typical HIT SRA profile
Interpretation of SRA results in this case: strong serotonin release at 0.1 and 0.3 U/mL UFH (97% and 99%), no release at 100 U/mL UFH
Atypical SRA feature 1: strong serotonin release at 0 U/mL heparin (96%), indicating heparin-independent platelet activation characteristic of aHIT
Atypical SRA feature 2: only partial inhibition by Fc receptor-blocking monoclonal antibody IV.3 (76% release at 0.1 U/mL UFH with IV.3), a novel serological phenotype
How the initial 'indeterminate' SRA result was reconciled with the diagnosis of aHIT through expert laboratory review
Importance of recognizing atypical SRA profiles to avoid missing the diagnosis of aHIT

sections.section_title: Treatment Strategy and Management of Severe Autoimmune HIT
sections.description: This section details the stepwise management of this severe case of aHIT, explaining the rationale for each therapeutic decision. It covers the initial switch from LMWH to fondaparinux and then to argatroban, the use of high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) for aHIT, monitoring of hypercoagulability markers, and the subsequent switch to therapeutic-dose fondaparinux with antithrombin supplementation.
subtopics: Immediate discontinuation of dalteparin (LMWH) and initial prophylactic-dose fondaparinux on POD5
Switch to therapeutic-dose argatroban (direct thrombin inhibitor): rationale, dosing (0.75 mcg/kg/min), and PTT target (55–85 s)
Rationale for argatroban over fondaparinux initially: shorter half-life preferred given recent stroke and severe thrombocytopenia
High-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG): rationale in aHIT, dosing (100 g × 2 days, then third dose), and expected platelet count response
Monitoring markers of HIT-associated consumptive coagulopathy: serial fibrinogen, d-dimer, and peripheral blood film for schistocytes
Evidence of progressive hypercoagulability on argatroban: falling fibrinogen (nadir 2.49 g/L on POD17), peak d-dimer around POD12, schistocytes from POD9–POD16
Suboptimal platelet count response to IVIG: nadir 13×10⁹/L (POD7), interim peak only 54×10⁹/L (POD14), indicating unusually severe aHIT
Switch from argatroban to therapeutic-dose fondaparinux (10 mg daily SC) on POD14: rationale including ease of administration and concern for insufficient hypercoagulability control
Antithrombin supplementation (1000 U) prior to fondaparinux initiation: rationale and pre-infusion AT level (0.70 U/mL)
General principles of HIT treatment: discontinuation of all heparin, alternative non-heparin anticoagulation, avoidance of platelet transfusions, role of IVIG specifically for aHIT

sections.description: This section covers the patient's gradual recovery, the evolution of laboratory findings over time, long-term anticoagulation management, and the key clinical and diagnostic lessons from this novel case of aHIT. It highlights how serial SRA testing confirmed the diagnosis and documented the evolution from aHIT to classic heparin-dependent HIT antibody profile as antibodies waned.
subtopics: Gradual platelet count recovery: 155×10⁹/L on POD62, 202×10⁹/L on POD87
Complete neurological recovery with resolution of stroke-related deficits
Duration of fondaparinux therapy (until POD65) and transition to oral apixaban 5 mg twice daily for long-term anticoagulation
Serial SRA results over months: persistence of strongly positive results, with evolution of SRA profiles

Later SRA profiles showing more characteristic aHIT pattern, and final sample (POD124) showing predominantly heparin-dependent HIT antibody profile (15% release at 0 U/mL, 100% at 0.3 U/mL UFH), reflecting waning of aHIT antibodies
Confirmation of aHIT diagnosis based on: evolving SRA profiles, final heparin-dependent pattern, and exclusion of alternative diagnoses
Clinical lesson 1: Preoperative heparin exposure can precipitate early-onset HIT (before POD5) following cardiac surgery
Clinical lesson 2: Severe thrombocytopenia (nadir 13×10⁹/L) with DIC-like features (falling fibrinogen, rising d-dimer, schistocytes) should raise suspicion for aHIT
Clinical lesson 3: Partial resistance to Fc receptor blockade (IV.3) on SRA is a novel serological phenotype of aHIT that should not be misinterpreted as excluding the diagnosis
Clinical lesson 4: Multimodal therapy (non-heparin anticoagulant plus IVIG) may be necessary for severe aHIT, with fondaparinux being an effective option for refractory cases
Clinical lesson 5: Awareness of atypical SRA profiles is essential to avoid missed diagnoses of aHIT with potential adverse consequences
